chapters.n: Mark opens with no birth story — he jumps straight to the good news. “Gospel” means “good news,” and his first line announces who Jesus is: the Christ (the anointed one) and the Son of God.

f.g: Greek euangelion — good news, a joyful announcement.

chapters.n: Mark quotes Malachi’s promise of a messenger sent ahead to prepare the way. John the Baptist is that forerunner, clearing the road for the Lord’s arrival.

f.w: I send my messenger before thy face

chapters.n: This line comes from Isaiah: a voice in the desert calling people to get ready for the Lord. Like workers smoothing a road for a coming king, John prepares hearts.

f.w: The voice of one crying in the wilderness

chapters.n: John baptized out in the wilderness and called people to repent — to turn their lives toward God — so their sins could be forgiven. His baptism looked forward to Christ.

f.g: Remission = release, forgiveness, the cancelling of a debt.

chapters.n: Crowds streamed out from the countryside of Judea and from Jerusalem itself. They were baptized in the Jordan River and openly admitted their sins.

f.g: The main river of Israel, flowing from the Sea of Galilee south to the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: John’s rough clothing and simple desert food made him look like the prophet Elijah, who also wore hair clothing and a leather belt. His appearance itself was a message.

f.g: Locusts (grasshoppers) were permitted food under the law of Moses.

chapters.n: John pointed away from himself. Untying sandals was a slave’s lowliest task, yet he said he wasn’t worthy even to do that for the One coming after him.

f.g: The strap or thong of a sandal.

f.w: There cometh one mightier than I

chapters.n: John’s baptism by water was real, but Jesus would bring something more: the gift of the Holy Ghost, which cleanses and transforms from within.

f.w: baptize you with the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: Jesus came south from his hometown of Nazareth and was baptized by John. Though sinless, he chose to be baptized to show obedience and set the pattern for all.
As Jesus came up out of the water, heaven opened and the Spirit came down on him in the sign of a dove. Here the Son, the Spirit, and (next verse) the Father all appear.
The Father’s voice declares his love and approval for his Son. Latter-day Saints see this scene as clear evidence that the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are three distinct beings.
Right after his baptism, the Spirit led Jesus out into the desert. Mark uses vivid, urgent words — “immediately,” “straightway” — to keep his story moving fast.

f.g: Strongly sends out. In the parallel account the Joseph Smith Translation adds that Jesus went into the wilderness “to be with God.”

chapters.n: For forty days Jesus faced Satan’s temptations, alone among wild animals, yet cared for by angels. Mark gives only a short summary; Matthew and Luke give details.
After John was arrested, Jesus began his public ministry in Galilee, the northern region where he grew up, announcing God’s kingdom.
Jesus’ message in a nutshell: God’s promised time has arrived, his kingdom is close at hand, so turn to God and trust the good news.

f.w: repent ye, and believe the gospel

chapters.n: Walking along the Sea of Galilee, Jesus noticed two brothers at work fishing — Simon (later called Peter) and Andrew.

f.g: A freshwater lake about 13 miles long in northern Israel, home to a busy fishing trade.

chapters.n: Jesus used their own trade as a picture of their new calling: instead of gathering fish, they would gather people to God.
They didn’t hesitate. Leaving their nets meant leaving their livelihood, a striking act of trust.
A little farther on, Jesus saw another pair of brothers, James and John, sons of Zebedee, repairing their nets in their boat.

f.g: Not the same as James the Lord’s brother; this James was later martyred.

chapters.n: They too followed immediately. The mention of hired servants suggests Zebedee’s fishing business was fairly successful — they gave up something real.

f.g: Paid workers — a sign the family business was not poor.

chapters.n: Capernaum, a fishing town on the north shore of the lake, became Jesus’ base. On the sabbath he taught in its synagogue, the local meeting house for scripture and prayer.

f.g: A town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee; Peter’s home was there.
A Jewish gathering place for reading scripture, prayer, and teaching.

chapters.n: People were amazed. The scribes usually taught by quoting earlier teachers, but Jesus spoke with his own authority, as one who truly knew.

f.g: Experts in the law of Moses who copied and interpreted scripture.

chapters.n: In the middle of the meeting, a man controlled by an evil spirit cried out. Darkness reacts when light enters the room.

f.g: An evil spirit, a follower of Satan.

chapters.n: The evil spirit recognized exactly who Jesus was — the Holy One of God — and feared him. Knowing who Jesus is is not the same as following him.

f.w: what have we to do with thee
f.g: An idiom meaning “leave us alone; we have nothing in common.”

f.w: I know thee who thou art

chapters.n: Jesus didn’t want testimony from demons. With a simple command he silenced the spirit and ordered it out.
The spirit left violently, shaking the man and shrieking, but it had to obey.
The crowd was stunned. Even evil spirits obeyed Jesus’ word. His power matched his teaching — both carried real authority.
News about Jesus spread quickly through all of Galilee.
Leaving the synagogue, Jesus and his four new disciples went to the home Simon and Andrew shared.
Simon Peter’s mother-in-law was in bed with a fever. This detail shows Peter was married. “Anon” means right away.
Jesus took her hand and raised her up, and she was healed so completely that she got up and served them. Healing led to service.
The sabbath ended at sunset. Then people were free to carry their sick, so they brought everyone who was ill or troubled by evil spirits.

f.g: Jewish days begin at sunset; carrying burdens was avoided until the sabbath ended.

chapters.n: It seemed as if the whole town crowded around the doorway of the house.
Jesus healed people with all kinds of illnesses. He would not let the evil spirits announce who he was; he chose his own timing for revealing himself.
After a long night of healing, Jesus rose before dawn to pray alone. Even the Son of God made private prayer a priority.
Simon and the others went searching for him.
When they found him, they reported that everyone was looking for him — expecting him to come back and keep healing in Capernaum.
Jesus instead chose to move on. His main purpose was to preach the gospel to as many towns as possible, not just to stay where he was popular.
He traveled through Galilee teaching in synagogues and freeing people from evil spirits.
A man with leprosy knelt and pleaded. He didn’t doubt Jesus’ power — only whether Jesus would want to help someone like him.

f.g: Someone with a serious skin disease; under the law he was unclean and had to live apart from others.

chapters.n: Moved with compassion, Jesus touched him — something nobody else would do for a leper. His answer, “I will,” shows the Savior’s willingness to heal.

f.g: Touching a leper normally made a person ceremonially unclean; here Jesus’ touch made the leper clean.

chapters.n: The healing was instant and complete.
Jesus firmly instructed him and sent him off quickly.
Jesus told him to keep quiet and to follow the law of Moses by showing himself to a priest, who would officially declare him clean and let him return to society.
The man couldn’t contain his joy and told everyone. As a result, crowds became so large that Jesus had to stay in open country — yet people still found him.
Back in Capernaum, word spread quickly that Jesus was staying at a house — probably Peter’s home.
So many people crowded in that even the doorway was blocked. Jesus used the moment to teach them God’s word.
Four friends carried a paralyzed man on a mat, hoping to bring him to Jesus.
Blocked by the crowd, the friends climbed onto the flat roof, dug through it, and lowered their friend down. Village roofs were often beams covered with branches and packed clay.
Jesus saw the friends’ faith and first addressed the man’s deepest need: forgiveness. Notice that other people’s faith helped bring this man to the Savior.
Some scribes in the room silently objected to what they had just heard.
Their reasoning was right that only God can forgive sins. Their mistake was failing to recognize that God was standing in front of them.

f.g: Speech that insults God or claims what belongs only to God.

f.w: who can forgive sins but God only?

chapters.n: Jesus knew what they were thinking without being told, and he answered their unspoken thoughts.
Anyone can claim to forgive sins — no one can see it. But a command to walk can be tested at once. Jesus was about to do the visible thing to prove the invisible one.
The healing would show that Jesus, the “Son of Man,” truly had divine authority to forgive. Son of Man was Jesus’ favorite title for himself.

f.g: Jesus’ usual title for himself, drawn from Daniel’s vision; Latter-day Saint scripture links it to God, the “Man of Holiness.”

chapters.n: Jesus spoke directly to the paralyzed man: get up, pick up your mat, and go home.
The man stood up and walked out with everyone watching. The crowd praised God, saying they had never seen anything like it.
Jesus went back out to the lakeshore, and crowds came to him there to be taught.
Levi (also called Matthew) collected taxes for the Roman-backed rulers. Tax collectors were often despised, yet Jesus invited him to follow, and Levi got up and did.

f.g: A tax booth, where duties on goods were collected.

chapters.n: Levi held a meal in his home, and many tax collectors and other people with bad reputations ate with Jesus and his disciples.

f.g: Reclined at a meal; guests lay on couches around a low table.
Tax collectors, seen as collaborators with Rome and often as cheats.

chapters.n: Religious leaders were shocked. Sharing a meal signaled friendship and acceptance, and they thought a holy man should keep away from sinners.

f.g: A Jewish group known for strict observance of the law and traditions.

chapters.n: Jesus compared himself to a doctor. A doctor goes to the sick, not the healthy. He came to call people who know they need help to repent and be healed.
Followers of John the Baptist and the Pharisees fasted regularly, and people asked why Jesus’ disciples didn’t.

f.g: Go without food (and drink) for a time, usually for religious devotion or mourning.

chapters.n: Jesus compared his presence to a wedding. Guests don’t fast while the groom is at the celebration — it’s a time for joy.

f.g: Wedding guests, especially the groom’s close friends.

chapters.n: A quiet hint of his coming death: when the groom is taken away, then his friends will fast and mourn.
A patch of new, unshrunk cloth will shrink and tear an old garment. Jesus’ gospel couldn’t simply be stitched onto old traditions.
Wine was stored in leather skins. New wine expands as it ferments; an old, stiff skin would burst. The new life Jesus brings needs new, flexible hearts.

f.g: Wineskins — leather bags, not glass bottles.

chapters.n: Walking through grain fields on the sabbath, the disciples picked heads of grain to eat. Picking by hand from a neighbor’s field was allowed by the law.

f.g: In KJV English, any grain — here wheat or barley, not American maize.

chapters.n: The Pharisees counted plucking and rubbing grain as harvesting — forbidden work on the sabbath under their traditions.
Jesus answered from scripture, reminding them of a time when hungry David and his men did something normally not allowed.
David ate the holy bread set out in the sanctuary, which only priests were meant to eat. Human need was put first. (The priest in 1 Samuel is Abiathar’s father, Ahimelech.)

f.g: Twelve loaves set before the Lord each sabbath in the tabernacle, later eaten by priests.

chapters.n: God gave the sabbath as a blessing for people — a day of rest and worship — not as a burden to enslave them.

f.w: The sabbath was made for man

chapters.n: As the one who gave the sabbath in the first place, Jesus has authority over how it should be kept.

f.g: The JST adds that the sabbath was given as a day of rest and that man was made to glorify God.

chapters.n: On another sabbath, Jesus was in the synagogue, and a man there had a shriveled, useless hand.
His critics weren’t there to worship. They watched closely, hoping he would heal on the sabbath so they could bring charges against him.
Jesus didn’t hide what he was about to do. He called the man to stand up in front of everyone.
Jesus asked a pointed question: is the sabbath a day for doing good or harm? Refusing to help someone in need is itself a kind of harm. His critics stayed silent.
Jesus felt both anger and sorrow at their stubborn hearts. He told the man to stretch out his hand, and it was made healthy.

f.g: Stubborn refusal to feel or understand.

chapters.n: The Pharisees immediately began plotting with the Herodians — political supporters of King Herod Antipas — to kill Jesus. Normally these groups were not allies.

f.g: Supporters of the Herod dynasty, which ruled with Rome’s blessing.

chapters.n: Jesus withdrew to the lakeshore, but huge crowds followed him from Galilee and from Judea to the south.
People came from far and wide — Jerusalem, Idumea in the far south, the lands east of the Jordan, and the coastal cities of Tyre and Sidon to the north.

f.g: Edom — the region south of Judea.
Gentile port cities on the Mediterranean coast, in today’s Lebanon.

chapters.n: So he wouldn’t be crushed by the crowd, Jesus had his disciples keep a small boat ready.
Because he had healed so many, people with diseases pushed forward just to touch him.
Evil spirits fell down before him and called him the Son of God. Ironically, demons recognized him before many people did.
Jesus sternly ordered them not to reveal who he was. He did not want testimony from evil sources.
Jesus went up into the hills and called those he chose to come to him.

f.g: Those he wanted — the choice was his.

chapters.n: He ordained twelve apostles. Their first calling was to be with him — learning from him — and then to be sent out to preach.
He gave them priesthood power to heal and to cast out evil spirits — the same works he was doing.
Simon was given the name Peter, from the Greek for “rock” (Cephas in Aramaic).
James and John were nicknamed “sons of thunder,” perhaps for their fiery, zealous personalities.

f.g: An Aramaic nickname Mark translates as “sons of thunder.”

chapters.n: More of the Twelve are listed. Matthew is Levi the tax collector. “Canaanite” here likely comes from an Aramaic word meaning “zealous,” not the ancient Canaanites.

f.g: Probably from Aramaic qan’an, “zealot”; Luke calls him Simon Zelotes.
Likely the same apostle Luke calls Judas the brother (or son) of James.

chapters.n: The list ends soberly with Judas Iscariot, the one who would betray Jesus. Then they went into a house.

f.g: Possibly “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea.

chapters.n: The crowds gathered again, so many that Jesus and his disciples couldn’t even eat.
Some of his family or friends, hearing about this, came to take charge of him, thinking he had lost his mind from overwork.
Official scribes from Jerusalem made a worse charge: that Jesus himself had Satan’s power and used it to drive out demons.

f.g: A name for the prince of devils — Satan.

chapters.n: Jesus answered with simple logic in short comparisons: why would Satan fight against his own forces?

f.g: Short comparisons or stories that teach a truth.

chapters.n: A kingdom torn apart by civil war will collapse.
So will a family that fights against itself.
If Satan were fighting himself, his rule would be ending — which was clearly not what they believed was happening.
You have to tie up a strong man before you can rob his house. By casting out devils, Jesus showed he had overpowered the “strong man,” Satan.
Jesus taught that God’s forgiveness reaches remarkably far — nearly every sin and even insulting words can be forgiven through repentance.
There is one exception: blasphemy against the Holy Ghost. Latter-day Saint teaching understands this as knowingly denying Christ after receiving a sure witness — a sin very few could commit.
Mark explains why Jesus said this: they were calling the Spirit’s work in him the work of an evil spirit.
Jesus’ mother and brothers arrived and, standing outside, sent word asking for him.

f.g: His brothers — sons of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus.

chapters.n: The crowd seated around him passed along the message that his family was asking for him.
Jesus asked a question to make a point about who truly belongs to him.
Looking at those listening to him, he called them his family. He wasn’t rejecting Mary; he was widening the circle.
Anyone who does God’s will becomes part of Jesus’ family. Discipleship creates family bonds as close as blood.

f.w: whosoever shall do the will of God

chapters.n: The crowd was so large that Jesus taught from a boat just off shore, using the water and the sloping beach like a natural amphitheater.
Jesus taught mostly through parables — simple stories from daily life that carry a deeper spiritual meaning for those willing to seek it.

f.g: From Greek parabolē, “a placing side by side” — a comparison.

chapters.n: “Listen!” Jesus begins with a farmer scattering seed by hand, a familiar sight in Galilee.
Some seed landed on the hard-packed path through the field, and birds ate it before it could sprout.
Some fell where a thin layer of soil covered rock. It sprouted fast because the soil warmed quickly.
But with no room for roots, the young plants dried up in the hot sun.
Other seed fell among thorn bushes, which grew up and crowded out the grain so it never produced a crop.
Some seed fell on good soil and produced a harvest — thirty, sixty, even a hundred times what was planted, an amazing yield.
Jesus invited everyone to really listen and think about what he meant.

f.w: He that hath ears to hear, let him hear

chapters.n: Later, in private, the Twelve and other followers asked him what the parable meant.
Jesus told his disciples they were being given the “mystery” — truths that God reveals — while those who weren’t seeking would hear only stories.

f.g: In scripture, a sacred truth that can be known only by revelation.

chapters.n: Jesus echoes Isaiah: some see but don’t perceive. Parables protect sacred truths from those who would mock them while rewarding those who seek.

f.w: seeing they may see, and not perceive

chapters.n: Jesus gently challenged them: if they didn’t understand this basic parable, how would they understand the others? This one is a key to the rest.
The interpretation begins: the seed is God’s word.
Hard-path hearers hear the word, but Satan snatches it away before it can take root.
Rocky-ground hearers receive the word eagerly and joyfully at first.
But their faith has no deep roots, so when trouble or persecution comes because of the gospel, they quickly give up.
Thorny-ground hearers also hear the word…
…but worries, the false promises of wealth, and craving for other things crowd out the word until it bears no fruit.

f.g: Wealth promises security and happiness it cannot truly give.

chapters.n: Good-ground hearers hear, accept, and produce real fruit in their lives — some more, some less, but all fruitful.
A lamp isn’t lit to be hidden under a basket or bed. Truth is meant to shine and be shared.
What is hidden for now will eventually come to light. The gospel was not meant to stay secret forever.

f.w: nothing hid, which shall not be manifested

chapters.n: Again Jesus urges careful, attentive listening.
Pay attention to what you hear. The measure you use — the effort and openness you give — determines what you receive. Those who listen will be given more.
Those who use what they receive gain more; those who neglect truth lose even what little they had. This is how spiritual learning works.

f.w: he that hath, to him shall be given

chapters.n: A parable found only in Mark: God’s kingdom is like seed a farmer plants in the ground.
The farmer goes about his normal days and nights, and the seed grows in ways he doesn’t fully understand.
The soil does the work in stages: first the stalk, then the head of grain, then full kernels. Spiritual growth is gradual, step by step.

f.w: first the blade, then the ear

chapters.n: When the grain is ripe, the farmer harvests immediately — a picture of the final gathering at the end of the world.
Jesus searches for another comparison to describe the kingdom of God.
The kingdom is like a mustard seed, tiny in size — proverbially the smallest seed people sowed.
Yet it grows into a large plant with branches big enough for birds to rest in its shade. Christ’s kingdom started small and would fill the earth.
Jesus taught many such parables, fitting his lessons to what his hearers were ready to understand.

f.w: as they were able to hear it

chapters.n: To the public he spoke in parables, but in private he explained everything to his disciples.
That evening Jesus told the disciples to cross to the other side of the lake — the eastern shore.
They left the crowd and took Jesus, still sitting in the boat he’d taught from. Other boats came along too.
A violent windstorm hit — common on the Sea of Galilee, which sits in a basin surrounded by hills — and waves swamped the boat.
Jesus, exhausted, was asleep on a cushion at the back. The terrified disciples woke him: don’t you care that we’re about to die?

f.g: The stern, the back of the boat.

chapters.n: Jesus stood up and commanded the wind and waves as if speaking to a living thing: “Peace, be still.” Instantly everything went calm.
Jesus asked why they were so afraid and still lacked faith. Faith in him is the cure for fear.
Now they were afraid in a new way — awed. Only God commands wind and sea. Who was this man?

f.w: What manner of man is this

chapters.n: Jesus and his disciples landed on the eastern side of the lake, a mostly Gentile (non-Jewish) region connected with the Decapolis cities.

f.g: People of the region around Gadara; some manuscripts read Gerasenes. The area was largely Gentile.

chapters.n: As soon as Jesus stepped out of the boat, a man possessed by an evil spirit came out from among the tombs to meet him.
The man lived in burial caves — a place considered unclean — and no one could restrain him, not even with chains.
He had often been shackled hand and foot, but he tore the chains apart and smashed the leg irons. No one could control him.
Day and night he roamed the hills and tombs, screaming and cutting himself with stones. Satan’s influence brings misery and self-destruction.
Yet when he saw Jesus from far away, he ran and knelt before him.
The spirit shouted Jesus’ true identity — Son of the Most High God — and begged not to be tormented. Evil spirits know Christ’s power and fear their coming judgment.

f.g: I solemnly beg you, I put you under oath.

chapters.n: Mark explains why: Jesus had already been commanding the spirit to leave the man.
Asked his name, the spirit answered “Legion” — a Roman army unit of thousands — because many spirits had taken hold of the man.

f.g: A Roman legion had roughly 5,000-6,000 soldiers.

chapters.n: The spirits pleaded not to be sent out of that region.
A large herd of pigs was grazing on the nearby hillside. Jews didn’t raise pigs, which were unclean under the law — another sign this was Gentile country.
The spirits begged to be sent into the pigs. Latter-day Saint teaching notes that Satan’s followers, having no bodies of their own, crave a body even an animal’s.
Jesus allowed it. The spirits entered the pigs, and about two thousand animals stampeded down a steep bank into the lake and drowned.
The herdsmen ran and spread the news in town and countryside, and people came out to see for themselves.
They found the once-wild man sitting calmly, dressed, and thinking clearly. Instead of rejoicing, they were afraid of such power.
Eyewitnesses told the newcomers what had happened to the man and to the pigs.
The townspeople begged Jesus to leave their area. Perhaps they cared more about their lost herd than a restored man.

f.g: Borders, territory — not just the seashore.

chapters.n: As Jesus got into the boat, the healed man begged to go with him.
Jesus didn’t allow it but gave him a mission instead: go home and tell your own people what the Lord has done and the mercy he showed you.
He became a witness throughout the Decapolis, the ten Gentile cities, telling what Jesus had done — and people were amazed. One healed person can prepare a whole region.

f.g: “Ten cities” — a league of Greek-style cities mostly east of the Jordan.

chapters.n: Jesus crossed back to the western (Jewish) side of the lake, and a big crowd gathered around him by the shore.
Jairus, a leader of the local synagogue — a respected man — fell at Jesus’ feet. Desperation humbled him.

f.g: Leaders who arranged synagogue services and cared for the building.

chapters.n: He begged Jesus to come lay his hands on his dying little girl so she would be healed and live. Laying on of hands is a pattern for priesthood blessings still today.
Jesus went with him, and the crowd pressed in on every side.
In the crowd was a woman who had suffered from constant bleeding for twelve years — the same number of years Jairus’s daughter had been alive.

f.g: A continual flow of blood, likely a menstrual disorder.

chapters.n: She had been to many doctors, spent everything she had, and only got worse. Her condition also made her ritually unclean and isolated from community worship.
Having heard about Jesus, she slipped into the crowd behind him and touched his clothes.
She thought that even touching his clothing would be enough to heal her.

f.g: Healed, made well; the Greek word also means “saved.”

chapters.n: The bleeding stopped at once, and she could feel in her body that she was healed.
Jesus felt power go out from him. He turned around in the crowd and asked who had touched his clothes.
The disciples thought the question was odd — everyone was bumping into him. But Jesus knew the difference between a casual touch and a touch of faith.
Jesus kept looking around to find the person.
The woman, frightened and trembling, came forward, knelt, and told him everything.
Jesus called her “Daughter” — the only time in the Gospels he addresses someone this way. He praised her faith and sent her off in peace, healed in body and restored to the community.

f.w: thy faith hath made thee whole

chapters.n: Just then messengers came with crushing news: Jairus’s daughter had died. Why bother the Teacher any longer?
Jesus overheard and immediately encouraged Jairus: don’t be afraid; just keep believing.
He took only Peter, James, and John with him. These three would also witness his transfiguration and his suffering in Gethsemane.
At the house there was loud commotion — people weeping and wailing. Professional mourners were customary at deaths.
Jesus asked why they were making such noise; the girl wasn’t dead but sleeping. For him, death is like sleep from which he can wake people.
The mourners mocked him. He sent them out and took only the parents and his three disciples into the room.
Taking her hand, Jesus spoke in Aramaic, his everyday language: “Little girl, I tell you, get up.” Mark preserves his exact words.
She got up at once and walked around. She was twelve years old. Everyone was utterly amazed.
Jesus told them firmly not to spread the news, and practically reminded them to give her something to eat — a tender, human touch.
Jesus returned to his hometown, Nazareth, with his disciples following.

f.g: His home region — Nazareth in Galilee.

chapters.n: On the sabbath he taught in the synagogue. People were amazed but puzzled: where did this local man get such wisdom and power?
They knew him as the carpenter, Mary’s son, with brothers and sisters still living in town. Familiarity made it hard for them to see him as more than ordinary.

f.g: Greek tektōn — a builder or craftsman working in wood or stone.
Likely the James who later led the Jerusalem church and wrote the Epistle of James.

chapters.n: Jesus noted a common pattern: prophets are often respected everywhere except among the people who knew them growing up.

f.w: A prophet is not without honour

chapters.n: Because of their unbelief, he did few miracles there — only healing a few sick people. Miracles follow faith; they don’t force it.

f.w: could there do no mighty work

chapters.n: Jesus was amazed at their lack of faith. He moved on and taught in the surrounding villages.
Jesus sent the Twelve out in pairs, giving them authority over evil spirits. Going two by two gave support and a double witness — still the missionary pattern today.
They were to travel light, taking only a walking stick — no traveler’s bag, food, or money — trusting God and the people they served.

f.g: A traveler’s bag for food and supplies.

chapters.n: They could wear sandals but not take an extra tunic.

f.g: Tunics — the long shirt worn next to the skin.

chapters.n: When a household welcomed them, they should stay there rather than move around looking for better lodging.
If a town rejected them, they were to shake the dust off their feet as they left — a solemn sign that they had done their duty and the town was responsible for its choice.

f.w: shake off the dust under your feet

chapters.n: The Twelve went out preaching that people should repent.
They cast out evil spirits and anointed many sick people with oil and healed them — an early example of priesthood blessings with consecrated oil.
Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, heard about Jesus. Haunted by guilt, he thought John the Baptist had come back from the dead.

f.g: Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great; he ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome.

chapters.n: Others had different ideas: maybe Jesus was Elijah, expected to return before the Messiah, or another prophet.
But Herod insisted: it’s John, the man I beheaded, come back to life.
Mark now flashes back to explain. Herod had arrested John because of Herodias, who had left Herod’s brother Philip to marry Herod.

f.g: A granddaughter of Herod the Great, and so also Antipas’s niece.

chapters.n: John had boldly told Herod that this marriage broke God’s law. Prophets speak truth even to rulers.
Herodias held a grudge and wanted John dead, but she couldn’t make it happen yet.
Herod respected and even feared John as a holy man. He protected him, was troubled by his words, yet liked to listen to him. Herod was torn.
Herodias’s opportunity came at Herod’s birthday banquet for his officials, military commanders, and Galilee’s leading men.
Herodias’s daughter (named Salome by the historian Josephus) danced and pleased the guests, and Herod rashly promised her anything she wanted.
He swore an oath, promising up to half his kingdom — a boastful phrase, since Rome actually controlled his lands.

f.w: unto the half of my kingdom

chapters.n: The girl asked her mother what to request. Herodias saw her chance: John’s head.
She hurried back and demanded John’s head right away on a platter.

f.g: Right now, at once (the phrase meant “immediately” in 1611).

chapters.n: Herod was very upset, but he didn’t want to break his oath or lose face in front of his guests. Pride led him to do what his conscience opposed.
He immediately sent an executioner, who beheaded John in prison.
The head was brought on a platter to the girl, who gave it to her mother. The gruesome detail shows the cost of John’s faithfulness.
John’s disciples came, took his body, and buried it with respect.
Back to the main story: the apostles returned from their mission and reported to Jesus everything they had done and taught.

f.g: Greek apostolos, “one sent forth” — a messenger with authority.

chapters.n: Jesus invited them to come away to a quiet place and rest. They were so busy they hadn’t had time to eat. The Savior cares about rest and renewal.

f.g: A lonely, uninhabited place — not necessarily sandy desert.

chapters.n: They left privately by boat for a secluded spot.
But people recognized them, ran ahead on foot around the shore from all the towns, and got there first.
Though tired, Jesus felt compassion. The people were like sheep with no shepherd — lost and unprotected — so he taught them.

f.w: as sheep not having a shepherd

chapters.n: Late in the day, the disciples pointed out the obvious: this is a remote place and it’s getting late.
They suggested sending everyone to nearby farms and villages to buy food.
Jesus told them, “You feed them.” They answered that it would cost two hundred denarii — about eight months’ wages for a laborer.

f.g: Two hundred denarii; one denarius was roughly a day’s pay for a laborer.

chapters.n: Jesus asked what they had. After checking, they reported five loaves and two fish. He started with what they could offer.

f.g: Small flat loaves, probably barley — the bread of the poor.

chapters.n: He had the people sit in groups on the green grass — a detail suggesting springtime.

f.g: Groups, like parties at a meal.

chapters.n: They sat in orderly rows of hundreds and fifties, like Israel organized in the wilderness.
Jesus looked up to heaven, blessed the food, broke the bread, and gave it to the disciples to distribute. The actions anticipate the Last Supper and the sacrament.
Everyone ate until they were full.
They gathered twelve baskets of leftovers — one for each apostle, and far more than they started with.
About five thousand men had eaten, not counting women and children, as Matthew notes.
Right away Jesus had his disciples get into the boat and head toward Bethsaida while he dismissed the crowd. John says the crowd wanted to make him king.

f.g: A fishing town on the north shore near where the Jordan enters the lake.

chapters.n: After sending the people off, he went up into the hills alone to pray.
By evening the boat was out in the middle of the lake, and Jesus was alone on shore.
He saw them straining at the oars against a headwind. Between about 3 and 6 a.m., he came walking on the water and was going to pass by them — perhaps to reveal himself as God passed by Moses.

f.g: Roughly 3:00-6:00 a.m. in the Roman system of night watches.

chapters.n: Seeing someone walking on the sea, they thought it was a ghost and screamed.
All of them saw him and were terrified. Jesus spoke immediately: “Take courage! It is I. Don’t be afraid.” “It is I” echoes God’s name, “I AM.”
He climbed into the boat and the wind stopped. They were completely astonished.
Mark explains frankly: they hadn’t understood the lesson of the loaves; their hearts were dull. Even close disciples needed time to understand fully who Jesus was.

f.g: Their minds were closed or slow to understand — not wickedness here, but spiritual dullness.

chapters.n: They landed at Gennesaret, a fertile plain on the northwest shore of the lake.

f.g: A plain south of Capernaum; the lake is sometimes called by this name too.

chapters.n: As soon as they stepped ashore, people recognized Jesus.
People ran throughout the area, carrying the sick on mats to wherever they heard he was.
Everywhere he went, people laid the sick in public places and begged to touch even the edge of his robe. All who touched him were healed.

f.g: The fringe or tassel that faithful Jews wore on the corners of their outer garment.

chapters.n: Pharisees and scribes came from Jerusalem — likely an official delegation sent to investigate Jesus.
They noticed some disciples eating without first performing the ritual hand-washing. The concern was religious purity, not hygiene.

f.g: Ritually unclean, “common” — not dirty in the modern sense.

chapters.n: Mark explains Jewish customs for his non-Jewish readers: the Pharisees carefully washed their hands before eating, following traditions passed down by earlier teachers.

f.g: The oral teachings of past rabbis, added to the written law of Moses as a “fence” around it.

chapters.n: After going to the market, where they might touch something unclean, they washed before eating. They also ritually washed cups, pots, copper vessels, and dining couches.

f.g: Probably the couches people reclined on to eat.

chapters.n: So they challenged Jesus: why don’t your disciples follow the elders’ tradition?
Jesus quoted Isaiah, calling them hypocrites — actors wearing a mask. They honored God with words while their hearts were far away.

f.w: This people honoureth me with their lips

chapters.n: Worship becomes empty when people teach human rules as if they were God’s commandments.
They had set aside God’s actual commands while clinging to man-made traditions like washing pots and cups.
With irony, Jesus said they were very skilled at rejecting God’s commandment in order to keep their own traditions.
Jesus gave an example. God’s law through Moses commanded honoring parents and treated cursing them as a grave crime.

f.w: Honour thy father and thy mother

chapters.n: But their tradition let a person declare money “Corban” — dedicated to God — and then claim it couldn’t be used to support aging parents.

f.g: A Hebrew word for an offering or gift devoted to God.

chapters.n: So they no longer let him help his father or mother. A religious-sounding vow became a loophole for neglecting family duty.
Their tradition cancelled out God’s word — and this was only one of many such examples.
Jesus called the crowd together and asked them to listen and understand.
His key teaching: what truly makes a person unclean isn’t food going in but what comes out of the heart.
Jesus invites everyone to really hear. (Many modern translations omit this verse because some early manuscripts lack it.)
In private, the disciples asked him to explain this saying.
Jesus was surprised they didn’t understand either. Food coming in from outside can’t make you spiritually unclean.
Food goes into the stomach, not the heart, and passes out of the body. Mark adds that this teaching declared all foods clean — a big change for early Christians.

f.g: Many read this as Mark’s comment that Jesus declared all foods clean.

chapters.n: What defiles a person is what comes out of them.
Sin begins in the heart: evil thoughts lead to sexual sin and violence.

f.w: out of the heart of men

chapters.n: The list continues: stealing, greed, malice, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, and recklessness.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom for envy or stinginess.
Greedy desire for what others have.

chapters.n: These things come from within and make a person unclean. The real battle for purity is in the heart.
Jesus traveled northwest into the Gentile region around Tyre and Sidon and tried to stay hidden in a house, but his fame made that impossible.

f.w: would have no man know it
f.g: The JST adds that he could not deny them, “for he had compassion upon all men.”

chapters.n: A woman whose young daughter was possessed by an evil spirit heard about him, came, and fell at his feet.
She was a Gentile — Greek-speaking, born in the Phoenician part of Syria. She begged Jesus to drive the demon out of her daughter.

f.g: A Phoenician from the Roman province of Syria.

chapters.n: Jesus tested her: the children (Israel) must be fed first; it isn’t right to give their bread to the dogs. The word means little house dogs, pets — a softer term.

f.w: Let the children first be filled

chapters.n: She answered with humble wit and faith: true, Lord — yet even the puppies under the table eat the children’s crumbs. She asked only for crumbs of his power.
Jesus honored her answer: go home; the demon has left your daughter.
She went home and found her daughter resting on the bed, free. Jesus’ power was not limited by distance or nationality.
Jesus took a long route back to the Sea of Galilee, going north through Sidon and then down through the Decapolis region east of the lake.
People brought a man who was deaf and could barely speak and asked Jesus to lay his hand on him.
Jesus took him away from the crowd and used touch and gestures the man could understand — fingers in his ears, saliva on his tongue — communicating care to someone who couldn’t hear.
Looking up to heaven, Jesus sighed deeply and said in Aramaic, “Be opened.”
At once the man could hear and speak clearly.

f.g: The tie or bond that held his tongue.

chapters.n: Jesus told them to keep it quiet, but the more he insisted, the more widely they told it.
People were overwhelmed: he does everything well! He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak — just as Isaiah foretold of God’s coming.

f.w: he maketh both the deaf to hear

chapters.n: Another huge crowd had gathered, probably in the mostly Gentile Decapolis region, and they had run out of food. Jesus called his disciples together.
Jesus felt compassion: the people had stayed with him three days and had nothing left to eat.

f.w: I have compassion on the multitude

chapters.n: If he sent them home hungry, they might collapse on the road, since some had come a long way.
The disciples asked how anyone could find enough bread out here in the wilderness — as if they had forgotten the feeding of the five thousand.
Jesus asked what they had. This time: seven loaves.
He had the people sit, gave thanks for the bread, broke it, and gave it to the disciples to serve.

f.g: Greek eucharisteō, the root of “Eucharist,” a name for the Lord’s Supper.

chapters.n: There were also a few small fish, which he blessed and had served as well.
Everyone ate and was satisfied, and seven large baskets of leftovers were gathered.

f.g: In KJV English, food of any kind.
A different, larger basket than in Mark 6 — the kind used to lower Paul over a wall.

chapters.n: About four thousand people ate. Then Jesus sent them home.
Right away he sailed with his disciples to the region of Dalmanutha, on the western shore of the lake.

f.g: A place of uncertain location; Matthew calls the area Magdala.

chapters.n: Pharisees came to argue and demanded a sign from heaven to prove his authority — a test, not a sincere request.

f.g: Testing him, trying to trap him.

chapters.n: Jesus sighed deeply. He would give no proof-on-demand to those who had already rejected his many miracles. Faith doesn’t grow from signs.
He left them, got back in the boat, and crossed to the other side.
The disciples had forgotten to bring bread; they had only one loaf in the boat.
Jesus warned them to beware of the “leaven” — yeast — of the Pharisees and of Herod. A little yeast spreads through a whole batch of dough; so does false teaching and worldly ambition.

f.g: Yeast or fermented dough; in scripture often a symbol of spreading corruption.

chapters.n: The disciples missed the point and thought he was scolding them for forgetting bread.
Jesus pressed them with questions. Were their minds still closed?

f.g: Are your minds still dull and unresponsive?

chapters.n: Echoing the prophets, Jesus asked: you have eyes and ears — don’t you see, hear, or remember?
He reminded them: when he fed five thousand with five loaves, how many baskets were left? Twelve.
And when he fed four thousand with seven loaves? Seven baskets.
Then why didn’t they understand? The one who fed thousands could surely handle a shortage of bread. The real danger was false teaching, not lunch.
At Bethsaida, people brought a blind man and begged Jesus to touch him.
Jesus led the man by the hand out of town, put saliva on his eyes, laid his hands on him, and asked if he could see anything.
The man looked up and said he could see people, but they looked like trees walking around — partly healed.

Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again, and the man’s sight was fully restored. Mark places this story right before Peter’s confession: the disciples, too, were coming to “see” Jesus clearly step by step.
Jesus sent him home and told him not to go back into the village.
Jesus and his disciples traveled north to the villages around Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked who people said he was.

f.g: A city near the springs of the Jordan at the foot of Mount Hermon, rebuilt by Herod Philip and named for Caesar.

chapters.n: They reported the public opinions: John the Baptist, Elijah, or one of the prophets. Everyone saw him as special, but not as who he really was.
Then Jesus asked them directly: “But who do you say I am?” Peter answered: “You are the Christ” — the Messiah, the Anointed One. A personal testimony matters more than public opinion.

f.g: Christ (Greek) and Messiah (Hebrew) both mean “Anointed One.”

chapters.n: He told them not to tell anyone yet, likely because many expected a political, military Messiah.
Now Jesus began to teach plainly that he, the Son of Man, must suffer, be rejected by Jerusalem’s leaders, be killed, and rise again after three days.

f.g: Leaders of the temple priesthood in Jerusalem.

chapters.n: He said this openly. Peter took him aside and began to scold him — he couldn’t accept a suffering Messiah.
Jesus turned, looked at the disciples, and rebuked Peter: “Get behind me, Satan!” Peter was unknowingly repeating Satan’s temptation to avoid the cross. He was thinking like man, not God.

f.g: Do not set your mind on, are not thinking about.

chapters.n: To everyone, Jesus taught the cost of following him: deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow. The cross was a vivid picture of total commitment.

f.g: The JST of the parallel explains this as denying oneself of all ungodliness and every worldly lust.

chapters.n: A paradox: those who cling to their life for themselves lose it, but those who give it to Christ and his gospel truly find it.
What good is gaining the whole world if you lose your own soul?

f.w: what shall it profit a man

chapters.n: Nothing is worth trading for your soul. It is beyond price.
Those who are ashamed of Jesus and his words in a faithless world will find him ashamed of them when he returns in his Father’s glory with the angels.

f.g: Unfaithful to God, as a spouse unfaithful to a covenant.

chapters.n: Jesus promised that some standing there would see God’s kingdom come with power before they died. Days later three of them saw his glory on the mount of transfiguration.

f.w: kingdom of God come with power

chapters.n: Six days later Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a high mountain, and his appearance was transformed before them, revealing his divine glory.

f.g: Changed in form and appearance by divine glory.
Traditionally Mount Tabor; many scholars suggest Mount Hermon near Caesarea Philippi.

chapters.n: His clothes shone with a whiteness no launderer on earth could produce. Mark’s homey comparison helps us picture heavenly glory.

f.g: A worker who cleaned and whitened cloth.

chapters.n: Elijah and Moses appeared and talked with Jesus — representing the prophets and the law, both pointing to Christ. Latter-day Saints believe they conferred priesthood keys on the three apostles here.

f.g: Elijah. The JST adds that John the Baptist was also there.

chapters.n: Peter, overwhelmed, offered to build three shelters — one each for Jesus, Moses, and Elijah — perhaps hoping to make this glorious moment last.

f.g: Tents or booths, like those used at the Feast of Tabernacles.

chapters.n: Mark gently explains that Peter didn’t know what to say because they were all terrified.
A cloud — a sign of God’s presence — covered them, and the Father’s voice declared: this is my beloved Son; listen to him. Not three equals: Jesus alone is the Son.

f.w: This is my beloved Son: hear him

chapters.n: Suddenly they looked around and saw only Jesus with them.
Coming down, Jesus told them to tell no one until he had risen from the dead. Then the vision would make sense.
They kept it to themselves but discussed among themselves what “rising from the dead” could mean.
Having just seen Elijah, they asked: why do the scribes teach that Elijah must come first, before the Messiah?
Jesus agreed that an Elias comes first to restore things — but scripture also says the Son of Man must suffer and be treated with contempt.
An Elias had already come — John the Baptist — and people treated him however they pleased. The role of “Elias” can apply to more than one forerunner.
Returning to the other disciples, Jesus found a large crowd around them and scribes arguing with them.
When the crowd saw Jesus, they were amazed and ran to greet him.
Jesus asked what they were arguing about.
A father spoke up: he had brought his son, who was possessed by a spirit that made him unable to speak.

f.g: A spirit that made him mute.

chapters.n: The spirit threw the boy into violent seizures, making him foam at the mouth, grind his teeth, and become rigid. The disciples had tried to cast it out but couldn’t.
Jesus expressed sorrow at the lack of faith around him — in the crowd and even in his disciples — and asked them to bring the boy.

f.g: Put up with you, bear with you.

chapters.n: When the spirit saw Jesus, it threw the boy into a convulsion; he fell and rolled on the ground, foaming at the mouth.
Jesus asked the father how long this had been happening. Since childhood, he replied. Jesus took time to listen.
The spirit had often thrown the boy into fire and water to kill him. The desperate father pleaded: if you can do anything, have pity and help us.
Jesus turned the question around: it isn’t a matter of whether I can — everything is possible for the one who believes.
The father cried out with tears one of scripture’s most honest prayers: “I believe; help my unbelief.” Imperfect faith brought to Christ is enough to begin.
As the crowd gathered, Jesus commanded the deaf and mute spirit to leave the boy and never return.
The spirit shrieked, shook him violently, and left. The boy lay so still that many said he was dead.
Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he stood. Mark’s language foreshadows resurrection.
Later, indoors, the disciples privately asked why they had failed.
Jesus said this kind requires prayer and fasting — a deeper spiritual preparation and reliance on God, not just a formula.
They traveled through Galilee quietly; Jesus didn’t want people to know where he was.
He was focusing on teaching the disciples about his coming betrayal, death, and resurrection on the third day.
They didn’t understand and were afraid to ask him to explain.
Back in Capernaum, Jesus asked what they had been arguing about on the road.
They were silent, embarrassed — they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest, right after he spoke of his suffering.
Jesus sat down like a teacher and called the Twelve. To be first in his kingdom, be last and serve everyone.
He took a small child, stood the child among them, and held him in his arms.
Welcoming a child — someone with no status — in Jesus’ name is welcoming him, and welcoming him is welcoming the Father who sent him.
John reported that they had stopped a man who was casting out devils in Jesus’ name because he wasn’t one of their group.
Jesus told them not to stop him. Someone doing good in his name isn’t likely to turn around and speak against him.
Whoever isn’t against us is for us. Jesus warned against narrow, jealous attitudes toward good done by others.
Even giving a cup of water to someone because they belong to Christ will be rewarded. Small acts of kindness matter to God.
But whoever causes a humble believer to stumble would be better off thrown into the sea with a huge stone around the neck. Leading others astray is serious.

f.g: A heavy grinding stone, often turned by a donkey.

chapters.n: Using strong exaggeration, Jesus taught that we must remove whatever causes us to sin, however dear. The JST explains the “hand” as a close friend who leads us astray.

f.g: Hyperbole — a dramatic figure of speech, not literal self-harm.
Greek Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a smoldering rubbish dump used as a symbol of punishment.

chapters.n: Jesus quoted Isaiah’s image of undying worms and unquenched fire to describe the lasting anguish of rejecting God.
The same principle applies to the foot: better to enter eternal life lame than to be lost whole.
This repeats the refrain for emphasis; some ancient manuscripts lack verses 44 and 46.
And to the eye: whatever we look at that leads us into sin should be shut out of our lives.
The refrain sounds a third time, driving home how serious sin’s consequences are.
Everyone will be tested and refined by fire, and sacrifices under the law were salted. Disciples are to be living offerings, purified by trials.

f.w: every sacrifice shall be salted with salt

chapters.n: Salt preserves and flavors, but salt that loses its taste is useless. Keep your covenant “saltiness” and live in peace with each other — a fitting end to an argument about greatness.
Jesus left Galilee for the last time, heading south toward Judea by way of Perea, the land east of the Jordan. Crowds gathered, and he taught them as usual.

f.g: Perea, the region east of the Jordan River, ruled by Herod Antipas.

chapters.n: Pharisees tried to trap him with a hot-button question: is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife? Herod Antipas, who ruled this area, had divorced to remarry — the issue that cost John his life.
Jesus sent them back to scripture: what did Moses command?
They answered that Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and send his wife away.

f.g: A written divorce certificate, which gave a woman legal freedom to remarry.

chapters.n: Jesus explained that Moses permitted divorce as a concession to hard hearts, not as God’s ideal.
From the very beginning, God created humanity male and female, designed for each other.
That’s why a man leaves his parents and is joined to his wife — marriage creates a new, primary bond.
The two become one. They are no longer two separate lives but one unit.
So what God has joined, people should not separate. Marriage is sacred, not a disposable contract.

f.w: What therefore God hath joined together

chapters.n: Back in the house, the disciples asked him more about this teaching.
Jesus taught that a man who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her — giving wives a dignity many laws then ignored.
The same standard applies to a woman who divorces her husband. Roman law allowed women to initiate divorce, so Mark’s readers needed this too.
Parents brought young children for Jesus to bless, but the disciples scolded them, thinking the Master was too busy for children.
Jesus was indignant. Let the children come; don’t stop them. God’s kingdom belongs to people like them.

f.w: of such is the kingdom of God

chapters.n: Anyone who doesn’t receive God’s kingdom with a child’s humble, trusting heart will not enter it.
Jesus took the children in his arms, laid his hands on them, and blessed them — a tender picture of how he values the youngest.
As he set out, a man ran up, knelt, and asked: “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” Matthew says he was young; Luke calls him a ruler.
Jesus questioned the casual use of “good.” Only God is truly good. Did the man realize whom he was speaking to?
Jesus listed commandments about treating others: no adultery, murder, theft, lying, or cheating, and honor your parents.

f.g: Don’t cheat or rob — perhaps a summary of the commandment against coveting.

chapters.n: The man sincerely said he had kept all these since his youth.
Jesus looked at him and loved him, then named the one thing he lacked: sell everything, give to the poor, and follow me. Jesus asked for the thing holding his heart.

f.g: Jesus’ invitation came from love, not harshness.

chapters.n: His face fell, and he went away sad, because he was very wealthy. The commandment revealed what he valued most.
Jesus looked around and told the disciples how hard it is for the wealthy to enter God’s kingdom.
The disciples were stunned — many thought wealth showed God’s favor. Jesus clarified: it’s hard for those who trust in riches.
With a vivid exaggeration, Jesus said a camel squeezing through a needle’s eye is easier than a rich person entering the kingdom.

f.g: Likely a deliberate, humorous impossibility — the largest animal through the smallest opening.

chapters.n: The disciples were utterly astonished: then who can be saved?
Jesus looked at them: by human effort it’s impossible, but nothing is impossible for God. Salvation is God’s gift. The JST adds that it is possible for those who trust in God and leave all for him.

f.w: with God all things are possible

chapters.n: Peter pointed out that they had left everything to follow him.
Jesus assured them that anyone who gives up home, family, or land for him and his gospel…
…will receive a hundred times as much now — a new family of believers, homes opened to them — along with persecutions, and eternal life in the world to come.

f.g: A realistic detail found only in Mark.

chapters.n: God’s kingdom will reverse the world’s rankings: many who seem first now will be last, and the last first.

f.w: many that are first shall be last

chapters.n: On the road up to Jerusalem, Jesus walked ahead with determination. The disciples were amazed and afraid. Again he took the Twelve aside to explain what was coming.

f.g: Jerusalem sits in the hills; travelers always “went up” to it.

chapters.n: In Jerusalem he would be handed over to the religious leaders, condemned to death, and given to the Gentiles — the Romans.
They would mock him, whip him, spit on him, and kill him, and on the third day he would rise again. This is the most detailed of his three predictions in Mark.
Right after this, James and John asked Jesus to grant whatever they would request.
Jesus asked them what they wanted.
They asked for the two highest honors — the seats on his right and left when he reigns in glory.
Jesus said they didn’t understand what they were asking. Could they drink his “cup” of suffering and be overwhelmed — “baptized” — by what he would endure?

f.g: A common biblical symbol for one’s destiny, especially suffering.

chapters.n: They said they could. Jesus agreed they would share his suffering — James was the first apostle martyred, and John endured long persecution.

f.w: Ye shall indeed drink of the cup

chapters.n: But places of honor are not his to hand out as favors; they belong to those for whom the Father prepared them.
The other ten were angry with James and John — probably because they wanted the same thing.
Jesus gathered them. Among the nations, rulers dominate and lord it over people.
It must not be so among his followers. Whoever wants to be great must serve.

f.w: so shall it not be among you

chapters.n: Whoever wants to be first must be everyone’s servant — even a slave to all.
Jesus himself is the model: he came to serve and to give his life as a ransom to free many. This verse sums up the meaning of his atoning death.

f.g: The price paid to free a captive or slave.

chapters.n: Passing through Jericho, the last town before the climb to Jerusalem, Jesus met a blind beggar named Bartimaeus sitting by the road.

f.g: Aramaic for “son of Timaeus,” as Mark explains.
An oasis city near the Jordan, about 15 miles east of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Hearing it was Jesus, he shouted, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” — a title for the promised Messiah-King.
People told him to be quiet, but he shouted even louder. Persistent faith refuses to be silenced.
Jesus stopped and asked for him. The crowd changed its tune: cheer up, get up, he’s calling you!
Bartimaeus threw off his cloak — maybe his only possession, used to collect coins — jumped up, and came to Jesus.
Jesus asked the same question he asked James and John: what do you want me to do for you? The blind man’s answer was simple: I want to see.

f.g: Greek rabbouni — “my master,” a very respectful address.

chapters.n: Jesus said his faith had healed him. He immediately saw — and followed Jesus on the road to Jerusalem. The blind man saw more clearly than many with sight.

f.g: “The way” also became an early name for following Christ.

chapters.n: This begins Jesus’ final week. Near Jerusalem, at the villages of Bethphage and Bethany on the Mount of Olives, he sent two disciples ahead.

f.g: A village about two miles east of Jerusalem, home of Mary, Martha, and Lazarus.
The ridge just east of Jerusalem, across the Kidron Valley.

chapters.n: He told them they would find a young donkey that had never been ridden, tied in the village ahead. An unridden animal was considered fit for sacred use.
If anyone asked, they were to say the Lord needed it and would send it back right away.
They found the colt tied by a door out on the street at a crossroads, just as Jesus said, and untied it.
Some bystanders asked what they were doing.
They gave Jesus’ answer, and the people let them go.
They spread their cloaks on the colt as a saddle, and Jesus sat on it — fulfilling Zechariah’s prophecy of a humble king riding a donkey.
People spread cloaks on the road and laid down leafy branches — a royal welcome like one given to kings.

f.w: spread their garments in the way

chapters.n: The crowds shouted “Hosanna!” and quoted a Passover psalm: blessed is he who comes in the Lord’s name.

f.g: Hebrew “save, we pray” — a cry for deliverance that became a shout of praise.

f.w: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord

chapters.n: They hailed the coming kingdom of David — expecting the Messiah to restore Israel’s kingdom. “Hosanna in the highest” calls on heaven to save.

f.w: the kingdom of our father David

chapters.n: Jesus entered Jerusalem and the temple and looked carefully at everything. Since it was late, he returned to Bethany with the Twelve for the night.
The next morning, leaving Bethany, Jesus was hungry.
He saw a fig tree in full leaf. Leaves usually signal some early fruit, but this tree had none. It wasn’t yet the main fig season.

f.w: the time of figs was not yet
f.g: The main harvest came later in summer; early small fruit often appeared with the leaves.

chapters.n: Jesus declared that no one would ever eat from it again. The disciples heard. The tree became an acted-out parable of Israel’s leaders: impressive leaves of religion, but no fruit.

f.w: No man eat fruit of thee

chapters.n: In the temple courts, Jesus drove out the merchants and buyers, overturned the money changers’ tables and the dove sellers’ seats.

f.g: They exchanged foreign coins for the Tyrian shekels required for the temple tax, often at a profit.

chapters.n: He wouldn’t let anyone use the temple courts as a shortcut for carrying goods.

Quoting Isaiah and Jeremiah, Jesus said God’s house was meant to be a place of prayer for all nations, but they had made it a hideout for robbers. The market filled the Court of the Gentiles, the one place non-Jews could pray.
The chief priests and scribes began looking for a way to kill him. They feared his popularity, because the people were captivated by his teaching.
Each evening Jesus left the city.
The next morning they passed the fig tree and saw it had withered from the roots up.
Peter remembered and pointed: Master, look — the fig tree you cursed has withered.
Jesus’ answer was simple: have faith in God.
Faith without doubt can move mountains. The Mount of Olives was right there, with the Dead Sea visible in the distance. Jesus used dramatic imagery to show what faith in God can do.
Pray believing you receive what you ask, and you will have it. True faith asks in harmony with God’s will.
When praying, forgive anyone you hold something against, so your Father in heaven can forgive you. Faith and forgiveness belong together.

f.w: forgive, if ye have ought against any

f.g: Standing was a common posture for Jewish prayer.

chapters.n: If we refuse to forgive others, we block God’s forgiveness of ourselves. (Some ancient manuscripts lack this verse.)
Back in the temple, the chief priests, scribes, and elders — the groups that made up the ruling council — confronted him.

f.g: Senior lay leaders, members of the Sanhedrin council.

chapters.n: They demanded: by what authority are you doing these things, and who gave it to you? They meant his actions in the temple.
Jesus answered with a question of his own, a common teaching method.
Was John’s baptism from heaven or just from men? The answer to that would also answer theirs, since John testified of Jesus.
They huddled: if we say from heaven, he’ll ask why we didn’t believe John.
If we say from men, the people will turn on us, because everyone believed John was a true prophet. They cared more about public opinion than truth.
So they claimed they didn’t know. Jesus replied that he wouldn’t tell them either. Those unwilling to accept truth they already have aren’t given more.

Jesus told a parable aimed at the temple leaders. A man planted a vineyard and equipped it fully, then rented it to tenant farmers. The setup echoes Isaiah’s “song of the vineyard,” where the vineyard is Israel.

f.g: A vat or pit where grapes were pressed.
Farmers, here tenant farmers who rented the land.

chapters.n: At harvest time the owner sent a servant to collect his share of the fruit, as the rental agreement allowed.
The tenants seized him, beat him, and sent him away with nothing.
He sent another servant; they stoned him, wounded his head, and treated him shamefully.
He sent more servants — some beaten, some killed. The servants represent the prophets God sent to Israel over the centuries.
Last of all, the owner sent his beloved only son, thinking surely they would respect him. “Beloved son” echoes the Father’s words at Jesus’ baptism.
The tenants plotted: this is the heir — kill him, and the vineyard will be ours. Jesus was describing the leaders’ plot against him.
They seized him, killed him, and threw his body out of the vineyard. Jesus would die outside Jerusalem’s walls.

f.w: cast him out of the vineyard

chapters.n: What will the owner do? He will come, destroy those tenants, and give the vineyard to others. Stewardship of God’s kingdom would pass to new leaders.
Jesus quoted a psalm: the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. The rejected Son would become the foundation of everything.

f.w: The stone which the builders rejected

f.g: The cornerstone or capstone — the most important stone in the building.

chapters.n: This reversal is the Lord’s doing, and it is wonderful to see.
The leaders knew the parable was about them and wanted to arrest him, but they feared the crowd, so they left.
Next they sent Pharisees and Herodians — normally rivals — to trap him with his own words.

f.g: Trap him, as a hunter snares an animal.

chapters.n: With flattery they asked: should we pay taxes to Caesar or not? Saying yes would anger Jewish nationalists; saying no would be treason against Rome.

f.w: regardest not the person of men
f.g: You don’t show favoritism or care about status.
Tax, especially the Roman poll tax.

chapters.n: Seeing through their act, Jesus asked why they were testing him and requested a denarius, the Roman coin used for the tax.

f.g: A denarius, a silver Roman coin worth about a day’s wage.

chapters.n: He asked whose image and inscription were on it. They answered: Caesar’s.

f.g: Inscription — the coin named Tiberius Caesar.

chapters.n: His brilliant answer: give Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and give God what belongs to God. The coin bears Caesar’s image; we bear God’s image — so we owe ourselves to him.

f.g: Give back, pay what is owed.

f.w: to God the things that are God's

chapters.n: Next came the Sadducees, a priestly group who accepted only the five books of Moses and denied any resurrection.

f.g: An aristocratic party tied to the temple priesthood.

chapters.n: They cited Moses’ law: if a man died childless, his brother should marry the widow to give the dead brother an heir.
They made up a story: seven brothers; the first married and died childless.
The second married her and died with no children, and the third the same.
All seven married her and died childless, and finally she died too.
Their trick question: in the resurrection, whose wife will she be? They meant to make resurrection look ridiculous.
Jesus said their error came from not knowing the scriptures or God’s power.
After the resurrection, marriages are not performed. Latter-day Saints understand from modern revelation that marriages must be sealed by God’s authority in this life to continue after it.

f.w: they neither marry, nor are given in marriage

chapters.n: Jesus answered from Moses — the scripture they accepted. At the burning bush God said, “I am the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” — present tense, long after they had died.

f.w: in the bush God spake unto him

chapters.n: God is the God of the living. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob still live to him. The Sadducees were badly mistaken.
A scribe who had heard the debate and was impressed asked sincerely: which commandment is the most important?
Jesus quoted the Shema, Israel’s daily confession of faith: “Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord.”

f.g: Hebrew Shema, “hear,” the first word of this central Jewish prayer.

chapters.n: Love God with everything you are — heart, soul, mind, and strength. This is the first commandment.

f.w: thou shalt love the Lord thy God

chapters.n: The second is like it: love your neighbor as yourself. No commandments are greater than these two.
The scribe agreed warmly: you’re right, Teacher. There is one God and no other.
He added that loving God and neighbor is worth more than all burnt offerings and sacrifices — echoing the prophets.

f.w: more than all whole burnt offerings

chapters.n: Jesus saw the man answered wisely and told him he was not far from God’s kingdom. After that, no one dared ask him more trick questions.
Now Jesus asked a question while teaching in the temple: how can the scribes say the Messiah is merely David’s son?
David, inspired, wrote: “The LORD said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.” David called the Messiah “my Lord.”

f.w: The LORD said to my Lord

f.g: A picture of total victory — enemies under one’s feet.

chapters.n: If David calls him Lord, how can he be only David’s descendant? The Messiah is both David’s son and David’s Lord — human and divine. The ordinary people loved listening to him.
Jesus warned against the scribes who loved flowing robes and respectful greetings in public.
They loved the best seats in synagogues and the places of honor at banquets.

f.g: The most honored places at the table.

chapters.n: They took advantage of vulnerable widows while putting on long prayers for show. Their judgment will be heavier because they used religion to exploit.

f.g: Possibly by mismanaging estates entrusted to them or exploiting widows’ generosity.

chapters.n: Jesus sat across from the temple treasury, where offering boxes stood, and watched people give. Many wealthy people gave large amounts.

f.g: Trumpet-shaped offering chests in the Court of the Women.

chapters.n: A poor widow put in two tiny copper coins — the smallest money in circulation.

f.g: Greek lepta, the smallest copper coins.
A quadrans, a tiny Roman coin — a fraction of a day’s wage.

chapters.n: Jesus called his disciples and said she had given more than all the others.

The rich gave from their surplus; she gave everything she had to live on. God measures gifts by the heart and the sacrifice, not the amount. She contrasts sharply with the scribes who “devour widows’ houses.”
Leaving the temple, a disciple marveled at its massive stones and magnificent buildings. Herod the Great’s rebuilt temple was one of the wonders of its age.

f.g: Some of the temple’s foundation stones were enormous — many tons each.

chapters.n: Jesus prophesied that every stone would be thrown down. This was fulfilled in AD 70 when Roman armies destroyed the temple.

f.w: there shall not be left one stone upon another

chapters.n: On the Mount of Olives, facing the temple, the first four disciples Jesus had called asked him privately about this.

f.g: Opposite the temple, with a full view of it.

chapters.n: They asked when it would happen and what sign would show it was about to be fulfilled. Jesus’ answer covers both Jerusalem’s fall and his Second Coming.
Jesus’ first concern: don’t be deceived.
Many would come claiming to be the Christ and would mislead many people.

f.w: many shall come in my name

chapters.n: Wars and rumors of wars must happen, but don’t panic — they don’t mean the end has arrived yet.
Nations will fight, and there will be earthquakes and famines. These are only the start of the birth pains — the first signs of a new age.

f.g: Literally “birth pangs” — painful but leading to new life.

chapters.n: Watch out: disciples would be handed over to councils, beaten in synagogues, and brought before governors and kings — giving them chances to testify of Christ.
Before the end, the gospel must be preached to all nations. This great missionary work is still unfolding.

f.w: the gospel must first be published among all nations

chapters.n: When arrested, they shouldn’t worry ahead of time about what to say. The Holy Ghost would give them the words.

f.w: it is not ye that speak, but the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: Persecution would split families: brothers, fathers, and children turning one another in to be killed.

f.w: the brother shall betray the brother

chapters.n: Disciples would be hated for Jesus’ sake, but those who endure to the end will be saved.

f.w: he that shall endure unto the end

chapters.n: When they saw the “abomination of desolation” Daniel spoke of — a desecration of the holy place — those in Judea should flee to the hills. Early Christians did flee Jerusalem before its destruction.

f.g: A horrifying desecration that brings ruin; fulfilled when Roman forces defiled and destroyed the temple.

chapters.n: Anyone on a flat rooftop should flee by the outside stairs without going in to grab belongings. There would be no time.

f.g: Flat roofs were used like patios, with stairs on the outside.

chapters.n: A worker in the field shouldn’t even go back for his cloak.
It would be especially hard for pregnant women and nursing mothers who couldn’t flee quickly.
Pray it doesn’t happen in winter, when rains swell rivers and travel is miserable.
The suffering of those days would be unmatched — a fearful time of distress.
If the Lord hadn’t shortened those days, no one would survive; but for the sake of his chosen people he cut them short.
If anyone says, “Look, here is Christ!” or “There he is!” — don’t believe it.
False Christs and false prophets will perform signs and wonders that could deceive even the chosen, if that were possible. Miracles alone don’t prove truth.
Be on guard — Jesus has told them everything in advance so they won’t be caught off guard.
After that distress, the sun will be darkened and the moon won’t shine. Jesus uses the prophets’ language for cosmic upheaval at his coming.
Stars will fall and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

f.w: the stars of heaven shall fall

chapters.n: Then people will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory — the Second Coming.
He will send angels to gather his chosen people from every direction and every corner of earth and heaven.
Learn from the fig tree: when its branches get tender and sprout leaves, you know summer is near. Unlike most trees in Israel, the fig loses its leaves in winter.

f.w: a parable of the fig tree

chapters.n: In the same way, when you see these signs, know that his coming is near — right at the door.

Jesus said this generation would not pass until all these things happen. The prophecies about Jerusalem were fulfilled within about 40 years; Joseph Smith—Matthew applies the phrase also to the generation that sees the last-days signs.
Heaven and earth will pass away, but Jesus’ words will never fail.

f.w: my words shall not pass away

chapters.n: No one knows the exact day or hour — not the angels, not even the Son during his mortal ministry — only the Father. Anyone who sets dates is mistaken.

f.w: of that day and that hour knoweth no man

chapters.n: So be careful, stay alert, and pray, because you don’t know when the time will come.
Jesus compares himself to a man going on a long journey who gives each servant authority and a task and tells the doorkeeper to stay alert.
So keep watch — you don’t know when the master will return: evening, midnight, at rooster crow, or dawn. These were the four Roman night watches.

f.g: The third watch of the night, roughly midnight to 3 a.m.

chapters.n: Don’t let him come suddenly and find you asleep. Within days, the disciples would fall asleep in Gethsemane.
His closing word is for everyone, not just the four: Watch! Live prepared every day.
Passover and the week-long Feast of Unleavened Bread were two days away. The chief priests and scribes were looking for a sneaky way to arrest and kill Jesus.

f.g: The yearly feast remembering Israel’s deliverance from Egypt, when the destroying angel “passed over” homes marked with lamb’s blood.

chapters.n: They wanted to avoid the feast itself, when Jerusalem was packed with pilgrims who might riot in Jesus’ defense.

At a dinner in Bethany at the home of Simon the leper (probably someone Jesus had healed), a woman broke open an alabaster jar of very costly perfume and poured it on Jesus’ head. John identifies her as Mary, sister of Martha.

f.g: A sealed flask of soft translucent stone; breaking its neck meant using it all.
Nard, a fragrant oil from a plant grown in the Himalayas — extremely expensive.

chapters.n: Some at the table were indignant: why waste such ointment?
It could have sold for over three hundred denarii — about a year’s wages — and the money given to the poor. They scolded her harshly.

f.g: 300 denarii, nearly a laborer’s yearly income.

chapters.n: Jesus defended her: leave her alone. She has done a beautiful thing for me.
There will always be poor people to help, and you should help them; but Jesus would not be with them much longer.

f.w: ye have the poor with you always

chapters.n: She did what she could, anointing his body ahead of time for burial. Whether she fully understood or not, her act honored his coming death.

f.w: She hath done what she could

chapters.n: Jesus promised that wherever the gospel is preached, her act of devotion would be told in her memory — and it still is.
In stark contrast, Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests to betray Jesus.
They were delighted and promised him money. Matthew says it was thirty pieces of silver. Judas began watching for a good opportunity.
On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when Passover lambs were sacrificed at the temple, the disciples asked where to prepare the Passover meal.

f.g: Lambs were slaughtered at the temple on the afternoon of the 14th of Nisan.

chapters.n: Jesus sent two disciples into the city to follow a man carrying a water jar — unusual, since women normally carried water, so he would be easy to spot.
They were to ask the homeowner where the Teacher’s guest room was for the Passover. Jesus had likely arranged this quietly to keep the location secret from Judas.

f.g: Master or owner of the house.

chapters.n: He would show them a large upstairs room, already furnished. There they should prepare.

f.g: An upstairs room, often used for guests and gatherings.

chapters.n: Everything happened just as Jesus said, and they prepared the Passover.
That evening Jesus arrived with the Twelve.
While they reclined and ate, Jesus said one of them, someone eating with him, would betray him. Betrayal by a table companion was especially painful.

f.w: One of you which eateth with me
