chapters.n: Grieved, they asked one by one, “Is it I?” Each was willing to examine himself.

f.g: The Greek expects the answer “no” — “Surely not I?”

chapters.n: Jesus said it was one of the Twelve, someone dipping bread in the same bowl with him.

f.w: dippeth with me in the dish
f.g: Bread was dipped in a shared bowl of sauce at the Passover meal.

chapters.n: The Son of Man would go to his death as scripture foretold, but terrible sorrow awaits his betrayer — better for him never to have been born.

f.w: as it is written of him

chapters.n: During the meal Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them: “Take, eat: this is my body.” He instituted the sacrament, a lasting reminder of his sacrifice.

f.g: The JST adds “in remembrance of my body,” showing it is a symbol.

chapters.n: He took the cup, gave thanks, and passed it to them, and they all drank.
“This is my blood of the new covenant, shed for many.” As blood sealed the old covenant at Sinai, Christ’s blood seals a new covenant.
Jesus would not drink wine again until he drinks it new in God’s kingdom. Latter-day Saint scripture says he will partake of the sacrament again with his disciples at his coming.

f.w: drink it new in the kingdom of God

chapters.n: After singing a hymn — likely the Hallel psalms traditionally sung at Passover — they went out to the Mount of Olives.

f.g: Probably from Psalms 113-118, sung at the Passover meal.

chapters.n: Jesus warned that they would all stumble and fall away that night, fulfilling Zechariah: strike the shepherd and the sheep scatter.
But a promise of hope: after he rose, he would go ahead of them to Galilee.

f.w: I will go before you into Galilee

chapters.n: Peter insisted that even if everyone else fell away, he never would.
Jesus told him that this very night, before the rooster crowed twice, Peter would deny him three times. Only Mark mentions “twice.”
Peter protested even more strongly: even if I must die with you, I will never deny you. All the others said the same.
They came to Gethsemane, a garden on the Mount of Olives. Jesus told the disciples to sit while he prayed.

f.g: Aramaic “oil press” — an olive grove where olives were crushed for oil.

chapters.n: He took Peter, James, and John further and began to be deeply distressed and troubled — overwhelmed, as Mark’s strong words show.

f.g: Deeply alarmed, overwhelmed with awe and distress.

chapters.n: He told them his soul was crushed with sorrow to the point of death and asked them to stay and keep watch.
Going a little farther, he fell to the ground and prayed that, if possible, this hour might pass from him. Here in Gethsemane the Savior began to take upon himself the sins and suffering of all.
“Abba, Father” — an intimate, trusting address. All things are possible for you; take this cup from me. Yet not my will, but yours. This is the heart of perfect submission.

f.g: Aramaic for “Father,” a warm, family word used by children and adults.

f.w: not what I will, but what thou wilt

chapters.n: He came back and found them asleep. He asked Peter — calling him Simon, his old name — couldn’t you stay awake even one hour?
Stay awake and pray so you won’t fall into temptation. The spirit is willing, but the body is weak. A tender acknowledgment of human limits.
He went away again and prayed the same words.
Returning, he found them asleep again; their eyes were heavy, and they didn’t know what to say to him.
The third time he said, “Enough — the hour has come.” The Son of Man was being handed over to sinners.
“Get up, let’s go. My betrayer is here.” Jesus went out to meet what was coming.
Immediately Judas arrived with an armed crowd sent by the chief priests, scribes, and elders, carrying swords and clubs.
Judas had arranged a signal: the man I kiss is the one — arrest him and take him away under guard.
He went straight to Jesus, said “Rabbi,” and kissed him warmly. A sign of love became the tool of betrayal.

f.g: A common greeting between a disciple and his teacher; Mark’s word suggests an affectionate kiss.

chapters.n: They seized Jesus and arrested him.
One bystander (John says it was Peter) drew a sword and cut off the ear of the high priest’s servant. Luke records that Jesus healed it.
Jesus asked why they came with weapons as if he were a violent bandit.
He had taught openly in the temple every day, and they never arrested him. But this was happening to fulfill the scriptures.
All the disciples abandoned him and ran away, just as he had foretold.
A young man wearing only a linen sheet was following, and the soldiers grabbed him. Many think this detail, found only in Mark, refers to Mark himself.

f.g: A sheet or light garment of linen.

chapters.n: He slipped out of the sheet and ran away naked. Even the last follower fled.
They took Jesus to the high priest, Caiaphas, where the chief priests, elders, and scribes — the ruling council — had gathered.

f.g: Caiaphas, high priest from about AD 18 to 36.

chapters.n: Peter followed at a distance into the high priest’s courtyard and sat with the guards warming himself by the fire. He was brave enough to follow, but from afar.

f.g: Here the courtyard of the high priest’s residence.

chapters.n: The council looked for testimony to justify a death sentence but couldn’t find any.

f.g: The Sanhedrin, the 71-member Jewish high court.

chapters.n: Many gave false testimony, but their stories didn’t match. The law required two witnesses who agreed.
Some stood up and testified falsely against him…
…claiming he said he would destroy this man-made temple and build another in three days without hands. They twisted his words about his own body.
Even then their testimony didn’t agree.
The high priest stood and demanded: aren’t you going to answer these charges?
Jesus stayed silent, like the lamb in Isaiah. Then the high priest asked directly: are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One? (“Blessed” was a reverent way to avoid saying God’s name.)
Jesus answered plainly: “I am.” And they would see the Son of Man seated at God’s right hand and coming with the clouds — combining Psalm 110 and Daniel 7.

f.w: sitting on the right hand of power

chapters.n: The high priest tore his robes — a dramatic sign of grief or outrage at blasphemy — and said no more witnesses were needed.

f.g: Tore his garments — a ritual reaction to hearing blasphemy.

chapters.n: “You have heard the blasphemy. What is your verdict?” They all condemned him as deserving death.
Some spat on him, blindfolded him, struck him, and mocked: “Prophesy!” — tell us who hit you. The guards beat him too. Ironically, his prophecies were being fulfilled at that very moment.
Meanwhile, below in the courtyard, one of the high priest’s servant girls came by.
Seeing Peter by the fire, she stared and said, “You were with Jesus of Nazareth too.”
Peter denied it, pretending not to understand, and moved out to the gateway. A rooster crowed.
The servant girl saw him again and told the bystanders, “He’s one of them.”
Peter denied it again. Soon the bystanders pressed him: surely you’re one of them — your Galilean accent gives you away.

f.g: Your accent matches — Galileans had a recognizable way of speaking.

chapters.n: Peter began to call down curses on himself and swear oaths: “I don’t know this man you’re talking about.” He wouldn’t even say Jesus’ name.

f.g: To invoke curses on himself if he was lying and to take oaths — not simply crude language.

chapters.n: Immediately the rooster crowed a second time. Peter remembered Jesus’ words and broke down weeping. His bitter tears began the repentance that would make him a mighty apostle.
At dawn the full council met to make its decision official, then tied Jesus up and handed him over to Pilate. Under Roman rule, only the governor could carry out a death sentence.

f.g: Pontius Pilate, Roman governor (prefect) of Judea about AD 26-36.

chapters.n: Pilate asked, “Are you the King of the Jews?” — a political charge, since a rival king meant rebellion against Rome. Jesus answered, “You say so,” affirming it but not in Pilate’s sense.

f.g: A guarded yes — “those are your words.”

chapters.n: The chief priests piled on accusations, but Jesus said nothing.
Pilate pressed him: don’t you have any answer? Look how many charges they bring.
Jesus still said nothing, and Pilate was amazed. His silence fulfilled Isaiah’s prophecy of the silent lamb.
It was customary at Passover for the governor to release one prisoner the people asked for.
A man named Barabbas was in prison with rebels who had committed murder during an uprising against Rome.

f.g: Aramaic “son of the father” — an irony, since Jesus is the true Son of the Father.

chapters.n: The crowd began calling for Pilate to grant the usual Passover release.
Pilate offered to release “the King of the Jews.”
He realized the chief priests had handed Jesus over out of jealousy.
But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to demand Barabbas instead.
Pilate asked what they wanted done with the one they called King of the Jews.
They shouted, “Crucify him!”

f.g: Execute by nailing or tying to a cross — Rome’s most painful and shameful punishment, reserved for slaves and rebels.

chapters.n: Pilate asked what crime he had committed, but they only shouted louder, “Crucify him!” An innocent man was condemned by a mob.
Wanting to satisfy the crowd, Pilate released Barabbas, had Jesus flogged, and handed him over to be crucified. The guilty went free while the innocent took his place — a picture of the Atonement.

f.g: Flogged with a whip of leather straps embedded with bone or metal — often brutal enough to kill.

chapters.n: Soldiers took him into the governor’s headquarters and gathered the whole cohort.

f.g: The governor’s official residence in Jerusalem.
A cohort — a unit of up to 600 soldiers.

chapters.n: They dressed him in a purple robe — the color of royalty — and pressed a crown woven from thorns onto his head, mocking his kingship.
They saluted him mockingly: “Hail, King of the Jews!” — a parody of “Hail, Caesar!”
They beat him on the head with a reed (a mock scepter), spat on him, and knelt in fake homage. One day every knee will bow in true worship.
When they finished mocking him, they put his own clothes back on and led him out to be crucified.
Jesus was too weak from the scourging, so soldiers forced Simon of Cyrene, a passerby from North Africa, to carry the cross beam. Mark names his sons, likely known to Mark’s readers.

f.g: From Cyrene, a city in today’s Libya with a large Jewish community.

chapters.n: They brought him to Golgotha, meaning “Place of a Skull,” just outside the city walls.
They offered him wine mixed with myrrh, a drink that dulled pain, but he refused it, choosing to face his suffering fully conscious.

f.g: A bitter aromatic resin used as a mild narcotic.

chapters.n: They crucified him and divided his clothing by casting lots, fulfilling a psalm of the suffering righteous one.
It was the third hour — about 9 a.m. — when they crucified him.

f.g: Hours were counted from about sunrise; the third hour was around 9 a.m.

chapters.n: The charge written above him read, “The King of the Jews.” Meant as mockery, it was the truth.

f.g: Inscription — a placard listing the crime.

chapters.n: Two rebels or robbers were crucified with him, one on each side — the places James and John had asked for in glory.

f.w: one on his right hand, and the other on his left

chapters.n: This fulfilled Isaiah’s words that he would be counted among the wrongdoers. (Many manuscripts lack this verse, but the prophecy is quoted in Luke.)

f.w: he was numbered with the transgressors

chapters.n: Passersby hurled insults, shaking their heads in scorn, mocking his supposed claim to destroy and rebuild the temple.
“Save yourself — come down from the cross!” But by staying on the cross he would save others.
The chief priests and scribes mocked too: “He saved others; he can’t save himself.” Unknowingly, they spoke a deep truth.

f.g: Not that he couldn’t, but that he wouldn’t — saving us required him to stay.

chapters.n: “Let the Christ come down now so we can see and believe.” Even the men crucified beside him insulted him.
At the sixth hour (noon), darkness covered the land until the ninth hour (3 p.m.). Creation itself mourned.

At three o’clock Jesus cried out in Aramaic the opening words of Psalm 22: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Latter-day Saint leaders have taught that the Father withdrew his Spirit so the Son could finish the Atonement alone.

f.g: Aramaic: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

chapters.n: Some bystanders misheard “Eloi” as a call for Elijah, whom Jews expected to come in times of need.
Someone soaked a sponge in sour wine and lifted it to his mouth on a reed, saying, let’s see if Elijah comes to take him down.

f.g: Sour wine, the cheap drink of soldiers.

chapters.n: With a loud cry, Jesus breathed his last. He voluntarily gave up his life; no one took it from him.
The temple veil — the heavy curtain closing off the Holy of Holies — was torn from top to bottom. God himself opened the way into his presence through Christ.
The Roman centurion standing in front of the cross saw how Jesus died and declared, “Truly this man was the Son of God.” A Gentile soldier makes the confession Mark’s Gospel has been building toward.

f.g: A Roman officer commanding about 80-100 soldiers.

f.w: Truly this man was the Son of God

chapters.n: Women watched from a distance, including Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and Joses, and Salome.

f.g: Mary from Magdala on the Sea of Galilee, healed by Jesus.
Probably the mother of James and John.

chapters.n: These women had followed Jesus in Galilee and supported his ministry; many others had come up with him to Jerusalem. When the men fled, the women stayed.

f.g: Served and supported him, including with their means.

chapters.n: Evening was coming on the day of preparation — Friday, the day before the sabbath. Bodies had to be buried before sunset.

f.g: The day to prepare for the sabbath — Friday.

chapters.n: Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council who was waiting for God’s kingdom, courageously went to Pilate and asked for Jesus’ body. It took real boldness to be associated with a crucified man.

f.g: A town in Judea, probably northwest of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Pilate was surprised Jesus was already dead — crucifixion often took days — and asked the centurion to confirm it.
Once the centurion confirmed the death, Pilate released the body to Joseph. Jesus truly died; his resurrection was not a recovery.
Joseph bought linen, took the body down, wrapped it, and laid it in a tomb cut out of rock. He rolled a stone across the entrance.
Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses watched where he was laid. They would be witnesses to the empty tomb, knowing exactly where it was.
When the sabbath ended Saturday evening, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought fragrant spices to anoint Jesus’ body — a final act of love for the dead.

f.g: Aromatic oils and spices used to honor a body and lessen the odor of decay.

chapters.n: Very early Sunday morning, as the sun was rising, they came to the tomb. Sunday became the Christian day of worship — the Lord’s Day — because of what happened next.

f.w: the first day of the week

chapters.n: On the way they wondered who would roll the heavy stone away from the entrance for them. They came anyway, trusting a way would open.
When they looked up, they saw the stone — a very large one — already rolled back.
Entering the tomb, they saw a young man in a white robe sitting on the right side, and they were alarmed. He was an angel; the JST and other Gospels speak of two angels.

f.g: An angel; the JST reads “two angels.”

chapters.n: “Don’t be alarmed. You are looking for Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen! He isn’t here. See the place where they laid him.” The center of the gospel in one sentence.
“Go tell his disciples — and Peter — that he is going ahead of you to Galilee.” Peter was named specially: the one who denied Jesus was not cast off.

f.g: Only Mark includes this tender detail.

chapters.n: The women ran from the tomb, trembling and bewildered, and at first said nothing to anyone because they were afraid. Many ancient manuscripts end Mark here.

Verses 9–20, the longer ending, summarize the resurrection appearances. The risen Lord appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had driven seven devils — a woman healed and redeemed became the first witness.

f.w: he appeared first to Mary Magdalene

chapters.n: She went and told those who had been with him, who were mourning and weeping.
When they heard he was alive and she had seen him, they didn’t believe her.
Later he appeared in a different form to two disciples walking into the country — the account Luke tells of the road to Emmaus.

f.g: So that they did not recognize him at first.

chapters.n: They went back and told the others, who still didn’t believe them.
Then he appeared to the eleven apostles as they ate and rebuked them for their unbelief and stubbornness in not believing the witnesses who had seen him risen.
He commissioned them: go into all the world and preach the gospel to everyone. This great commission drives the Church’s missionary work today.

f.w: Go ye into all the world

chapters.n: Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; whoever refuses to believe will be condemned. Faith and baptism go together.

f.w: He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved

f.g: Condemned — stopped in progress, under judgment.

chapters.n: Signs will follow believers: in Christ’s name they will cast out devils and speak in new tongues. Signs follow faith; they don’t create it.

f.w: these signs shall follow them that believe

chapters.n: They will be protected from serpents and poison and will lay hands on the sick for healing. Paul survived a viper bite on Malta. This is promised protection, not a call to test God.
After speaking to them, the Lord was taken up into heaven and sat at God’s right hand — the place of power and honor.

f.w: sat on the right hand of God

chapters.n: The apostles went out and preached everywhere, and the Lord worked with them, confirming their message with miracles. The gospel that began in Mark 1:1 now goes to the world.
